articles.title: Former cricket captain Colin Cowdrey's son wins £500,000 from neighbour after legal battle over £3.85 million country home; dispute began over a strip of land that included part of his private tennis court
articles.summary: Jeremy Cowdrey, son of former England cricket captain Colin Cowdrey, has won a costly legal battle with his neighbour after a dispute over a strip of land
articles.body: Jeremy Cowdrey, son of former England cricket captain Colin Cowdrey, has won a costly legal battle with his neighbour after a dispute over a strip of land disrupted the sale of his £3.85 million country home in Kent. The disagreement, which began when Vanessa Gibson acquired land containing part of his private tennis court, escalated into a court case involving allegations of harassment, malicious falsehood and attempts to extract money. A judge ruled in Cowdrey’s favour, awarding him compensation and ordering Gibson to pay a substantial contribution towards his legal costs.A strip of land triggered the £3.85 million country home disputeThe dispute centred on Crowbourne Farm, a substantial country property in Goudhurst, Kent, bought by Jeremy Cowdrey in early 2022. As reported by The Independent in February 2025, the Grade II-listed farmhouse sits within more than 10 acres and includes a guest cottage, studio, barn, workshop, wine cellar, stables, woodland and two lakes, alongside a tennis court.Cowdrey’s disagreement with Vanessa Gibson, who lives in a nearby barn conversion, began after she bought a strip of land that included part of his tennis court. Gibson argued that the court extended onto land she owned, creating a boundary dispute between the neighbours.The Independent reported that Cowdrey eventually agreed to fence off the disputed section and relinquish any claim to it. The arrangement was intended to settle the disagreement, but the relationship between the two neighbours deteriorated further as Cowdrey attempted to sell the property.Why did the planned sale fall apartCowdrey put Crowbourne Farm on the market in June 2023, initially advertising it for more than £3.25 million. According to The Independent, he claimed that several prospective buyers had been discouraged by Gibson’s correspondence and that he had agreed a £3.85 million sale with a couple before they withdrew.His legal team alleged that Gibson continued to present the boundary issue as unresolved, despite the earlier agreement. They also accused her of raising concerns about restrictive covenants, flooding and the property’s utility connections.The Standard reported that Cowdrey believed his neighbour was making allegations in an attempt to extract money from him while he was trying to sell the estate. At a preliminary hearing, his barrister argued that the correspondence was designed to jeopardise the transaction and pressure him into paying her.Gibson disputed the allegations. She maintained that her concerns were legitimate and related to the land she owned, including flooding that affected both properties.What did the judge decide about the neighbour's conductThe case proceeded to Central London County Court, where Judge Jane Evans-Gordon considered Cowdrey’s claims of malicious falsehood and harassment. The Independent reported in November 2025 that the judge found Gibson’s conduct had gone beyond protecting her own interests.The court decided that the earlier boundary dispute had been settled and that Gibson had attempted to conceal her intention to interfere with the sale. Her claims about continuing disagreements involving the tennis court, utility services and land covenants were found to be false.The judge said Gibson’s actions between March 2022 and June 2023 were motivated by an improper purpose, specifically causing financial loss by preventing Cowdrey from selling Crowbourne Farm unless he paid the amount she wanted.The judge considered that Gibson had concealed her purchase of the strip of land until she could use ownership to seek significant payment. While she was entitled to protect her interests, the court found that her conduct had crossed the line into a form of blackmail or maliciousness.How much compensation did Jeremy Cowdrey receiveCowdrey had sought damages after the agreed £3.85 million sale collapsed. He argued that the property would have been worth around £3.7 million without Gibson’s allegations and claimed the difference between that figure and the failed sale price.Judge Evans-Gordon awarded him £150,000, together with interest, for the financial loss associated with the failed transaction. She also gave £9,000 in damages for the oppressive and unreasonable harassment he had experienced. The total compensation came to approximately £159,000 before interest.Why did the legal bill take the award beyond £500,000The financial consequences grew further when the parties returned to court over legal costs. The Independent reported in November 2025 that Gibson had been ordered to pay £360,000 towards Cowdrey’s legal expenses, including VAT, as an initial payment before the full costs were assessed.That amount was on top of the £159,000 compensation award. Together, the sums brought the immediate financial order to roughly £519,000, explaining reports that Cowdrey had won around £500,000 from his neighbour.Cowdrey’s barrister argued that Gibson should bear the substantial legal costs because of the way she had conducted the litigation. The judge ordered a significant portion of the costs to be assessed on an indemnity basis, a more demanding approach to costs recovery. Gibson told the court she did not have the money to pay the bill, according to The Independent.What restrictions were placed on future contactThe November 2025 hearing also addressed how the neighbours would communicate in future. Gibson gave legally binding undertakings setting out how and when she could contact Cowdrey.Judge Evans-Gordon warned that breaching those commitments could amount to contempt of court. The Independent reported that she explained such a breach could carry a fine or imprisonment of up to 2 years.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: CMAT: Pop star joins Philomena Begley in surprise Belfast appearance
articles.summary: Philomena Begley was honoured with the Lifetime Achievement Award in recognition of her 64-year career.
articles.body:
Irish star CMAT made a surprise appearance at an award ceremony in Belfast on Wednesday.

The pop-star joined Philomena Begley, one of Irish country music's most loved and celebrated entertainers, on stage at the NI Music Prize.

Begley was honoured with the Lifetime Achievement Award in recognition of her 64-year career.

The country music legend performed the hit Blanket on the Ground alongside CMAT.

The NI Music Prize, an annual event celebrating music in Northern Ireland, was marking its 15th anniversary on Wednesday at Ulster Hall.

Begley's award was presented by BBC broadcaster Hugo Duncan, a longtime friend of the musician.

When Begley went on to perform Blanket on the Ground she invited CMAT, who had made a surprise appearance at the ceremony, to join her on stage.

At a concert in Belfast earlier this year, CMAT, whose real name is Ciara Mary-Alice Thompson, gave a shout-out to Begley, thanking the country legend.

Reacting to the shout-out in October, Begley told the Good Morning Ulster programme that she had never met her but had "heard so much about her".

"It's hard to beat the new generation, it's great to see them all doing well."

Begley added that she was "over the moon" to win the award.

Begley said she did not know what reaction to expect at the awards ceremony, but that she was "looking forward to it".

Charlotte Dryden, CEO of Oh Yeah Music Centre, who were the organisers of the NI Music Prize, said that seeing Begley and CMAT together "was something really special".

"We've had some incredible moments at the NI Music Prize over the years, but I don't think we've ever experienced an atmosphere quite like that," she said.

Philomena Begley is one of the island's most loved entertainers.

An unrivalled interpreter of country music, she has delighted audiences on stages all over the world and collaborated with country greats like Porter Wagoner and Billie Jo Spears, who first released Blanket on The Ground.

From humble beginnings in Pomeroy, County Tyrone, Begley had a simple, but happy childhood as one of eight children in a close-knit, traditional and musical family.

She always loved to sing, but had no plans of pursuing a career in music.

Begley accidentally entered the world of country music at a local dance, when she was called on stage as a dare to sing a song with the Old Cross Céilí Band.

An instant hit, she was asked to fill in as cover for someone who had taken ill in the band and suddenly became swept up in the 1960s dance-hall circuit.

In 1975, Begley was granted permission to record her own version of Blanket on the Ground from US country music star Billie Jo Spears who had released it earlier that year as the title track from the album of the same name.

Begley's version went to number five in the Irish charts and sparked some friendly rivalry between the pair.

Over the years, they became close friends, sharing many of the same hits and performing together on several occasions.

Blanket on the Ground remains one of Begley's most popular songs to this day.

Begley has captivated crowds on stages all over the world, performing everywhere from Wembley Stadium to Nashville, Tennessee.

In 1978, she was invited by Porter Wagoner, the man who introduced Dolly Parton to the world, to perform at the Grand Ole Opry, Nashville's legendary home of country music.

Here she rubbed shoulders with the stars of global country music and even received a standing ovation for her performance of Blanket on the Ground.

It was fitting recognition for her contribution to country music in Ireland and beyond.

Dillon Boyd, from The Spirit of '49 Dungannon Swifts supporters club, said it all started after the Pomeroy woman's song was played on the bus radio on an away trip and "the whole place just took off".

Speaking to BBC News NI ahead of the Irish Cup final, Ms Begley said she was "shocked, but delighted" with the response.

The Swifts went on to win the final , holding their nerve against Cliftonville to secure a 4-3 penalty shootout win after a 1-1 draw after extra time.

At a victory parade after the final , the Queen of Country joined players on stage for a rendition of 'Blanket on the Ground'.

There were a number of other artists honoured on Wednesday, including Joshua Burnside, who won the PPL Album of the Year award for It's Not Going to Be OK.

Belfast band Chalk, meanwhile, celebrated a double win: the group was awarded Single of the Year for Pain, as well as MCD Live Act of the Year.

Kaidi Tatham was named PRS for Music NI Creator of the Year.

Polar Bolero won the public-voted BBC Introducing in Northern Ireland Artist of the Year award.

Composer and musician Neil Martin won Outstanding Contribution to Music Award.

The full list of NI Music Prize award winners was:

Neil Martin: Outstanding Contribution to Music Award

Philomena Begley: Lifetime Achievement Award

articles.title: TODAY’s Make-Ahead Thanksgiving: Chefs Share Freezer-Friendly Recipes for a Stress-Free Holiday
articles.summary: For Make-Ahead Thanksgiving, chefs provide fridge- and freezer-friendly recipes so all you have to do is thaw, reheat and finish your dishes for a stress-free holiday.
articles.body: Picture this: It’s Thanksgiving Day. Your family is on their way over. If it were any other year, you’d be running around, multitasking like crazy — chopping, stirring, whisking, folding, mashing, crimping, basting — but this year is different. You’re completely calm, cool and collected. Why? Because you’ve prepared everything in advance. That could be you if you start planning now. Two weeks out from the big day, we’re here to help, with some of our favorite, most-trusted chefs. Follow along and you could have Martha’s sweet potato casserole in your fridge alongside your thawed turkey and Jernard Wells’ cranberry honey mustard sauce, as well as Giada’s pasta bake, Rick Martinez’s cheesy Brussels sprouts and Erin French’s icebox cake in your freezer. Fast-forward to Thanksgiving and all you have to do is cook your bird, pull your dishes out of the freezer or fridge, thaw, reheat, finish and serve. That means a holiday with a lot less time stressing and scrambling, and a lot more time enjoying family and friends (perhaps with a cocktail in hand?). Make-Ahead Sides Sage adds a savory note to sweet potatoes in Martha’s comforting sweet potato casserole. Best of all, it can be made two days before the meal. Make-ahead tips: The potato puree can be refrigerated for up to two days. Make the breadcrumbs and sprinkle them on top just before baking. (The dish may need to bake for 10 to 15 minutes longer if cold.) Giada’s cozy, cheesy pasta bake is everything we love about comfort food, with sweet winter squash, tender broccolini and a golden, crunchy topping. It’s a wonderful side dish for the holidays because you can assemble it ahead of time, freeze it and simply bake it when you’re ready to serve. Make-ahead tips: This dish can be frozen for up to three months. For the crispiest topping, freeze the casserole without the breadcrumbs and add them just before baking. Marcus’ take on an irresistible Southern classic is warmed up with ginger, cardamom and chili, and paired with honey butter, earning a spot on your Thanksgiving table. Make-ahead tips: After letting the loaf cool completely, cut it into thick, 1-inch slices. (That way, you can thaw only what you need, and slices reheat more evenly than a whole loaf.) Wrap each slice tightly in plastic wrap, then put the slices in a zip-top freezer bag and press out as much air as you can. Label the bag with the date and freeze for up to three months. The butter also freezes well for up to three months. Thaw it in the refrigerator overnight, then let it sit out 15 minutes before serving so it’s spreadable. Eric calls these mashed potatoes, which are inspired by the ones served at a NYC restaurant called Anton’s, “the best mashed potatoes I’ve ever had.” They’re called “whipped potatoes” to reflect their light, fluffy texture. For the velvetiest mash, he says, you can mash the potatoes as much as you want, preferably with a fork. Make-ahead tips: These potatoes can be made in advance and stored in a resealable container in the refrigerator for up to three days and in the freezer for up to three months. To reheat them, cook them in a saucepan with some milk over low, stirring until warmed through. From frozen: Thaw them first in the refrigerator overnight. It’s not often you find a make-ahead dish with leafy greens that can maintain its veggie bite, especially after facing the freezer. That’s where Brussels sprouts come in to save the day. The hearty little heads won’t turn to mush through cold or heat. Even better, Rick’s comforting casserole is also packing in plenty of melty cheese and crispy pancetta. Make-ahead tips: This dish can be made ahead and frozen for up to three months. Using plastic wrap, you can freeze it in the casserole dish, then remove the frozen block from the dish to keep in the freezer. The day before Thanksgiving, remove all the plastic wrap from the frozen casserole, return the frozen block to the baking dish, cover and thaw in the refrigerator. Add the cheese right before baking and bake according to the recipe. If you’re a jalapeño popper person, you’re gonna love Rick’s recipe. You get the heat from the jalapeños, the salty umami and a little bit of smoke from the bacon, and then that creamy cheese filling. To give it more of a Thanksgiving-y feel, he tops it with crispy cornbread crumbles. Make-ahead tips: Same as the above! Once thawed, make the cornbread topping, add it to the mac right before baking and bake according to the recipe. Stuffing’s great and all, but a savory bread pudding (aka strata) is where it’s at when it comes to making it ahead. You want to allow the bread chunks to really soak up the custard mixture so it stays moist when you bake it. It’ll come out like a creamy stuffing, flecked with caramelized onions, crispy bacon and thyme, which no one will be mad about. Make-ahead tips: Freeze all components individually. Prep the caramelized onions, put them in a plastic bag and freeze them. Prep the bread cubes, put them in a plastic bag and freeze them. Prep the bacon, put it in a plastic bag and freeze it. Then, the day before Thanksgiving, thaw all the parts out in the fridge. When you’re ready to cook, dump them in the casserole dish along with the eggs, heavy cream and seasonings, mix until combined, and bake per the recipe. Do you top your sweet potato casserole with marshmallows or pecans? Well, why not both? The combination creates a candy-like topping to crack into and reveal the silky sweet potatoes underneath. Make-ahead tips: Line your casserole dish with heavy-duty foil, leaving plenty hanging over the sides. Assemble your casserole and freeze until solid. Lift the entire frozen casserole out of the dish, wrap it tightly and return it to the freezer. (Your dish is now free to use for something else!) The day before you plan to cook, remove the casserole from the freezer, then bake it per the recipe. This decadently cheesy gratin is a wonderful way to get your greens on Thanksgiving. Leafy chard, earthy mushrooms and fragrant onions mingle with nutty Gruyère and bold raclette cheese in this elevated casserole. Best of all, you can prepare it ahead of time to make holiday entertaining easier. Make-ahead tips: Allow the gratin to cool, then cover and refrigerate for up to three days. Alternatively, wrap the entire dish in a large freezer bag and freeze. If frozen, transfer to the refrigerator the day before Thanksgiving to thaw. On Thanksgiving Day, bake until the gratin is bubbling and browned. Make-Ahead Soup and Sauces To make good gravy, you usually have to wait until the bird is done before you can get started with those coveted pan drippings. Daniel’s make-ahead recipe uses turkey wings to cut out the waiting time while keeping all the savory flavor. You get all the rich poultry and roasted vegetable flavor in a fraction of the time. Make-ahead tips: The gravy can be refrigerated for up to four days or frozen for up to a month. On Thanksgiving Day, simply bring it to a gentle simmer, add your pan drippings and enjoy. Jernard’s sauce brings a sweet, tart and tangy twist to the Thanksgiving table with very little effort. Cranberries and honey balance the Dijon beautifully, making it a perfect partner for turkey, ham or roasted chicken. He also loves spreading it on a leftover turkey sandwich the next day. Make-ahead tips: You can make this sauce a few days ahead (up to a week) to let the flavors come together. It can also be stored in the freezer for up to three months. Daniel purées fresh chestnuts with celery root, leeks, onions, apples, nutmeg, thyme and heavy cream to create what is, essentially, every fall flavor packed into one bowl. Make-ahead tips: The soup can be cooled completely and stored in a covered jar in the refrigerator for three to four days, or frozen for up to a month. Bring the soup back to a boil before serving. Make-Ahead Desserts When dessert’s been cleared and the coffee’s been poured, a bowl of Erin’s almond- and ginger-flecked chocolate bark at the center of the table is all it takes to keep the conversation going until the last candle snuffs itself out. Make-ahead tip: Store in an airtight container at room temperature for up to two weeks. Jernard’s pie brings together tender cinnamon apples, buttery crumble and a sweet caramel finish with just a touch of sea salt. A store-bought crust and prepared caramel sauce keep it easy, and the crumble topping means there is no lattice to weave. Make-ahead tips: Cover and refrigerate the apple filling and crumble separately for up to 24 hours. Fit the crust into the metal pie pan, cover and refrigerate separately. Keeping the filling out of the crust until baking helps prevent a soggy bottom. Erin’s icebox pie is your make-ahead, no-heat dessert that you just have to pluck from the freezer in an effortless gesture at the end of the meal. It is cool and creamy with a hint of nostalgia. And this ginger and cream version complements berries and stone fruits. She suggests making this pie the day before you plan to serve it, then slicing it straight from the freezer. Make-ahead tips: For best results, add the whipped cream and cherry compote just before serving. Let the pie sit at room temperature for a few minutes before slicing or serving, if needed. Store any leftover cherry compote separately in an airtight container in the refrigerator. Want more recipe inspiration? Join our Thanksgiving virtual event with Start TODAY dietitian Natalie Rizzo on Tuesday, Nov. 17.

articles.title: Mississippi's Masala moment: A historic Black victory in America’s Deep South
articles.summary: TOI correspondent in Washington: Thirty-five years after Mira Nair, then pregnant with Zohran Mamdani, brought Mississippi Masala to screen, exploring the
articles.body: TOI correspondent in Washington: Thirty-five years after Mira Nair, then pregnant with Zohran Mamdani, brought Mississippi Masala to screen, exploring the unlikely romance between an Indian woman and a Black man in America's Deep South, America’s poorest state has scripted a plot twist that Hollywood might have considered improbable: electing its first Black US senator in more than 150 years.In a remarkable real-life sequel, Democrat Scott Colom, a civil rights attorney, has defeated Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith, by a narrow 4600 votes margin to become Mississippi's first Black US senator since Reconstruction, when the beaten Confederacy was briefly undergoing a democratic transformation.The symbolism is difficult to overstate: Mississippi has the highest proportion of Black residents of any American state, approaching 40 per cent. Yet the state has not elected a Black senator since Blanche Bruce, who entered the Senate in 1875 and served until 1881. Hiram Revels, the first Black American senator, had also represented Mississippi, in 1870. What followed was nearly a century of segregation, poll taxes, literacy tests, lynchings and violent resistance to Black political participation as Mississippi became synonymous with some of America's ugliest racial chapters.There is an Indian connection to this history that goes beyond Nair's movie, which explored the unlikely relationship between Mina (Sarita Chowdhury), the daughter of Indian immigrants expelled from Idi Amin's Uganda, and Demetrius, an African American carpet cleaner played by Denzel Washington early in his career. In 1935, Howard Thurman, the African American theologian and civil rights intellectual who grew up in the segregated South, travelled to India with a delegation and met Mahatma Gandhi in February 1936. Their discussions about racial oppression, freedom and non-violence helped transmit Gandhian ideas into the American civil rights movement. Thurman subsequently influenced Martin Luther King Jr., who drew deeply from the Gandhian philosophy of non-violent resistance.Even more strikingly, Indian freedom fighter and social reformer Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay spent 18 months travelling across America between 1939 and 1941. On a journey through the segregated South, she encountered the indignity of racial segregation on an American train in next door Louisiana, where a conductor challenged her presence in a whites-only carriage. Refusing to move, she recognised a kinship between the struggles of African Americans and Indians against systems of racial and imperial domination. Her observations, later recorded in America: The Land of Superlatives, offer a remarkable Indian perspective on the American South.Colum is very much in that Gandhian mold. A civil rights lawyer, municipal judge, and three-term District Attorney, he was given no chance in the election considering Trump had won the state by a whopping 23 per cent in 2024 and Hyde-Smith had won her previous election by seven points. Virtually every poll had classified her seat as safely Republican. But he refused to budge.In fact, such was Hyde-Smith’s hubris that she declined repeated invitations to debate Colom, sneering that he would not be able to fill a room if she was not present. Trump himself may have sensed some trouble though when polls showed the race narrowing in the final days, making his first visit to Mississippi in seven years to campaign for her. "I'm here because Cindy's doing great, but I just got to make sure. I can't take a chance,” he said.On Wednesday, Colum took his chance and drove Hyde-Smith out of the Senate with a stunning victory that was built on kitchen table issues rather than bloviating about ballrooms. A 7th generation Mississippian, his campaign masterstroke was a 30-sec ad built around Hyde-Smith's response to complaints about soaring beef prices: consumers, she suggested, had plenty of other proteins to choose from. Colom's ad, echoing the “let-them-eat-cake” smackdown, featured incredulous Mississippians delivering the devastating rejoinder: rather than choose another protein, they would choose another senator.On Thursday, Democrats were dancing in the aisles even as MAGA minions were panicking at the prospect of Colum becoming a “national threat” to the Republican Party as one Fox News commentator put it -- bigger than Democratic Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Colom himself offered a characteristically restrained response to suggestions that he could become a national political star: Mississippi first; no masala please.You use AI every day. articles.title: Suspected bomb hoax threats force fresh evacuations of Italian schools
articles.summary: Schools across Italy have received bomb threats for the second day in a row, sparking fresh panic and evacuations.
articles.body:
Schools across Italy have received bomb threats for the second day in a row, sparking fresh panic and evacuations.

Some 1,800 schools, from Milan in the north to Sicily in the south, reported receiving a similar threat to one that created chaos in Italy on Wednesday - even though no devices have been found anywhere.

The Italian government has advised schools that "in the absence of concrete evidence beyond the simple receipt of a mass email indicating a danger, buildings must not not be evacuated".

Schools in Scotland and Northern Ireland received threats on Wednesday, too. It is unclear whether the incidents are connected.

On Thursday morning, a bomb alert at a Calais rail station delayed international and national train services in northern France.

The latest incidents follow a series of bomb hoaxes last week against airports and airlines in a number of European countries.

Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings.

Wednesday's email threat - sent to 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 Italian state schools - was said to be from a certain "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan".

Some officials say it originated in Taiwan.

A similar message sent to Italian schools on Thursday, again signed by Mikhail Andropov, is said to have been sent from the account of a teacher in the Philippines whose account is believed to have been hacked.

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has spoken of "a strategy intended to cause alarm and concern".

Many parents, though, are concerned and have been demanding clarity and action from the government.

La Repubblica newspaper reports that protests have been held against a decision by the headmaster of a secondary school in Rome who did not take any action, saying she had realised the threatening message to contain typos and therefore be "fake".

According to the newspaper, protesters want new national guidelines to be issued.

articles.title: Schools, libraries and parents face 'difficult decision' over David Walliams books
articles.summary: Some schools remove the children's author's books from their libraries after allegations against him.
articles.body:
Some schools have removed David Walliams books from their libraries following the publication of allegations against the best-selling children's author and comedian.

"Head teachers are already making difficult decisions about whether or not these books should remain on the bookshelves of libraries at the moment," said Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders.

"I'm aware from several of our members that they've already taken the decision to take them off their shelves."

Walliams sold more than 50 million copies of books including Gangsta Granny and Billionaire Boy. He has denied allegations of sexual misconduct and abuses of power.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Mr Di'Iasio urged the government to give schools national guidance, so they are "not leaving this open to one or two head teachers making one decision and others making a different one".

Darren Morgan, head of Kings Road Primary School in Manchester, told the programme that he has taken the decision to remove Walliams' publications.

The stories have been useful to promote reading, but "when there are these allegations it's really difficult to keep these books on the shelves", he said.

Steve Chalke, head of Oasis Academies, which runs more than 50 schools, said it was impossible to stop children seeing the current stories about Walliams.

"So when a child wanders into a school and into the library and sees his name or perhaps sees his photograph on a book, it can be very traumatising for some children," he said.

Author Chloe Combi, who has written about "how it feels to be young in modern Britain" and Generation Z, said banning Walliams' books is not appropriate, and could mean that important conversations about him "get swept under the carpet".

"I think by talking about it and what has happened - and the responsibility of parents to have that conversation with their kids - that actually makes more sense," she told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"I'm totally sympathetic with schools for withdrawing him and bookshops withdrawing him as an individual decision. But the point is, none of that is going to erase what's happened."

The Department for Education has been asked for comment.

'Extremely complex and stressful situation'

Retailers including Waterstones, TG Jones, and The Works, say they will no longer sell Walliams' books, and his publisher HarperCollins cut ties with him in September.

Public libraries have also faced calls to remove his books.

Librarians' body CILIP said it "recognises that dealing with challenges made to books or other resources can be an extremely complex and stressful situation for library staff".

Decisions about stocking books are made by local councils.

Among them, Kent County Council said it had no plans to remove Walliams' titles from its libraries.

"The starting point is that books should be available to readers unless their content is unlawful," a spokesperson said.

"Decisions about library stock are not made through blanket bans on individual authors. Collections are regularly reviewed and refreshed to reflect factors such as reader demand, condition and relevance of stock."

Surrey County Council said that demand for Walliams' books had "fallen significantly in recent years", but his titles are "not illegal" and "remain available for readers to borrow".

Camden Council in north London said it was putting Walliams' books in storage.

A spokesperson told the Camden New Journal: "We are committed to making Camden a safer place for women and girls, to challenging harmful attitudes, and promoting healthy relationships.

"Following these allegations, we believe the most appropriate action is to remove these books from display."

On Tuesday, ITV News and the Guardian published reports alleging that Walliams has been accused of sexual misconduct by several women, including some who accused him of "grooming" them when they were teenagers.

In a letter to journalists published by the paper, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

articles.title: Ex-Bond producer named Buckinghamshire film school's president
articles.summary: Barbara Broccoli is succeeding David Puttnam in the role in February.
articles.body:
A producer whose credits include the James Bond movies has been announced as the first female president of a film school.

Barbara Broccoli will take over the role at the UK's National Film and Television School (NFTS) in Beaconsfield, Buckinghamshire, in February, succeeding Oscar-winning producer David Puttnam.

She has produced nine Bond films with her half-brother, Michael G. Wilson, before it was announced in February that Amazon MGM Studios had gained creative control.

Puttnam, whose credits include Chariots of Fire, The Killing Fields and Midnight Express, said he was "over the moon" that such a "hugely respected figure" was succeeding him.

The National Film School was established in 1971 by director Colin Young, taking over the Beaconsfield site with an initial intake of about 25 students.

In 1982 the institution was renamed the National Film and Television School to reflect its expanding curriculum.

Puttnam, who has been involved with the school for over 50 years, said it was a "lovely job" to have and that he had tried never to interfere.

He added that Broccoli's decision to take up the role was a "wonderful thing for the school".

Puttnam will take on an honorary role as president emeritus.

News of Broccoli's appointment comes ahead of the opening in January of the Cubby Broccoli Building at the school's Beaconsfield campus.

The building is named after Broccoli's father, the producer Albert R. "Cubby" Broccoli, who established the James Bond franchise.

The school said its expansion will provide 25,000 sq ft of additional teaching space, house new courses in costume design and hair and make-up, expand apprenticeship opportunities and provide purpose-built accessible student accommodation for the first time in its history.

articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns amid spy scandal and market loss
articles.summary: Tech giant’s market value drops below $4 trillion after Huang steps down following espionage and affair allegations.
articles.body:
Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO of tech giant Nvidia following his reported affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a company executive.

The firm’s market value fell below $4 trillion for the first time since 2025 following the announcement, capping a volatile week as Huang’s scandals rocked the company, which supplies most of the chips powering advanced artificial intelligence (AI) technology. The stock slid roughly 10 percent in early trading as US markets opened on Thursday. The tech-heavy Nasdaq was down 0.6 percent.

The company appointed Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer and executive vice president, as interim CEO on Thursday.

The firm also added its first-ever board chair, Harvey C Jones, who has been a venture investor for the last three decades.

Nvidia’s board met on Wednesday night to discuss ousting Huang, whose relationship with an alleged Chinese spy triggered investigations by the FBI, the United States Congress and the California-based chip maker. Nvidia is also facing a shareholder class-action lawsuit.

The alleged Chinese intelligence asset, Alice Huang, is a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, Nvidia’s primary business partner in Southeast Asia. Founded in 2023, Megaspeed has been investigated over whether it helped Chinese companies access its $4.8bn stock of powerful Nvidia chips.

The affair has raised national security concerns in the US, which restricts chip sales to China over concerns that the Chinese military, intelligence agencies or companies could use the advanced technology.

Huang, 63, is Nvidia’s cofounder, president and CEO. A close ally of US President Donald Trump, he has pushed to ease US restrictions on chip exports to China. Trump said earlier this week that Huang told him he had “absolutely no idea” that he was in a relationship with an intelligence operative.

Huang owns about 3.6 percent of Nvidia’s stock, making him one of the richest people in the world. He is a powerful figure in the AI industry, which has driven record stock market and wider economic gains. The company is set to report quarterly earnings on Tuesday.

Aleksandar Tomic, associate dean for strategy, innovation, and technology at Boston College, told Al Jazeera that the “resignation of Jensen Huang will have an outsized effect compared to a similar event at another large corporation given the relatively flat structure of Nvidia.”

But he said that Nvidia, an AI bellwether, “is in a very strong position” that will enable the company to transition from Huang’s leadership. Tomic called Huang’s resignation a “speed bump” for the company.

“Nvidia is a strong company with a strong product and this is a sudden event, not a product of corporate struggle,” he said. “It may take some time to figure out the succession process, but Nvidia can handle it as they approach it from the position of strength.”

Nvidia’s board, which hired a law firm to investigate the affair with Alice Huang, met to decide Huang’s fate on Wednesday shortly after The New York Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with an Nvidia vice president who reports to him.

Nvidia’s stock has tumbled since the scandal erupted, falling to a 14-year low, the Reuters news agency reported.

articles.title: Baghdad’s first Jewish museum draws crowds to rediscover Iraq’s Jewish past
articles.summary: Iraq’s Jewish community numbered about 150,000 in 1947. Between 1950 and 1952, around 125,000 Iraqi Jews were airlifted to Israel.
articles.body: Dozens of Iraqis visit Baghdad’s first Jewish museum each day to view faded school certificates, handwritten documents and family photographs. The exhibits offer a glimpse into a once integral part of Iraqi life that has all but disappeared. The museum occupies the historic Shamash Jewish School, founded in 1928 on Al-Rashid Street, a prominent thoroughfare in Baghdad. Iraq’s Jewish community opened the museum last month in a rare public celebration of the country’s Jewish heritage. Inside the restored building, visitors move between display cases holding personal photographs, identity cards, graduation certificates and records of Jewish students who studied at the school, which the Jewish philanthropist Yacoub Shlomo Shamash founded. A brass menorah sits above archival documents, and another seven-branched candelabrum is displayed against polished wooden panels. Framed black-and-white portraits line the walls, among them an image of Sassoon Heskel, a Baghdad-born Jew who served as Iraq’s first finance minister after the modern state was founded in 1920. The museum also pays tribute to prominent figures from Iraq’s Jewish heritage, including celebrated singer Salima Murad. Born into a Jewish family in Baghdad, Murad rose to fame in the 1920s and 1930s as one of Iraq’s most acclaimed vocalists, known for performing the traditional Iraqi Maqam, a classical Arabic musical form, and lighter popular songs. Her career reflected the prominent role Jews once played in Iraq’s cultural life. No Jewish visitors have come yet, but Iraqis have arrived in significant numbers since the museum opened, said Ammar al-Tamimi, legal representative of the Jewish community in Iraq. Nabil Abdul Hameed, a 71-year-old Baghdad resident who has visited twice, said he did not believe the museum existed until he saw it himself. He first visited alone and later returned with his daughter, a physician, and her children. “I saw people’s interest in this subject, and I hope it is a seed of goodness that grows in the future, because the Jews were among the founders of this country,” he said. “I hope those in charge will think about bringing the Jews back. The Jews have property, history and heritage. I wish they would come and take part in the revival of the country.” Tamimi said the museum was created to preserve the school’s memory after demographic and economic changes transformed the surrounding area. The building is now part of a commercial district with warehouses and can no longer operate as a school, he said. The project was led by Khalida Fouad Eliyahu, a 64-year-old dentist born in Baghdad to a Jewish family who heads Iraq’s small remaining Jewish community. She wants to restore other landmarks linked to the country’s centuries-old Jewish presence, Tamimi said, adding that all funding for the museum came from Jewish community resources. Historian Saadi al-Iraqi welcomed the opening and called for wider preservation of Iraq’s Jewish heritage. “This step is wonderful and beautiful, and we want more,” he said. “I want the synagogues to open. We want their houses of worship to open too.” A dwindling community Under Ottoman rule and into the first half of the 20th century, Jews made up roughly a fifth of Baghdad’s population. Jewish communities in the Middle East stretch back over 2,500 years, but anti-Jewish violence, fanned by Arab nationalism, started to sweep through the region in the early 1940s, gradually driving out most Jews. Iraq’s Jewish community numbered about 150,000 in 1947. Between 1950 and 1952, around 125,000 Iraqi Jews were airlifted to Israel. Nowadays, official Iraqi figures show only a handful of Jews remain in Baghdad, living quietly for safety reasons, while around 90 Jews of Kurdish origin still live in the Kurdistan region. The legacy of Iraq’s Jewish community remains visible across the capital, from old commercial districts to riverside villas, where six-pointed Stars of David are etched into stucco facades.

articles.title: Legal challenge to UK's largest approved solar farm rejected
articles.summary: Two councils launched a claim for a judicial review after the approval of Springwell Solar Farm.
articles.body:
A legal challenge to the UK's largest currently approved solar farm has been rejected by the High Court.

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) approved Springwell Solar Farm, between Lincoln and Sleaford, in April, saying it would help "bring down bills for good".

Lincolnshire County Council and North Kesteven District Council sought to overturn the decision, arguing the project would harm rural communities and landscapes.

County Council leader Sean Matthews said he was disappointed with the decision, while developer EDF said it was pleased, adding it would "make important contributions to the UK's security of electricity supply".

Developer EDF said the 800 MW project, which will cover 1,280 hectares (3,163 acres), would provide a major contribution to the UK's future energy mix, powering 180,000 homes.

Earlier this year, the councils launched a claim for a judicial review of the government's decision to approve the plans.

Judicial reviews are court proceedings that examine the lawfulness of a decision or action made by a public body, according to the Courts and Tribunals Judiciary .

On Wednesday, the High Court dismissed the councils' request to move forward with a judicial review.

Matthews said: "Given the size of this development, I'm disappointed that our councils will not have the opportunity to present a case at a full hearing.

"The impact of this development won't be felt in London, where all these decisions have been made. Rather, residents across dozens of rural communities now face the likelihood of huge industrial solar farms appearing on their doorstep.

"Despite the outcome, we firmly believe that standing up for our communities is the right thing to do."

Leader of North Kesteven District Council, Richard Wright, added: "It was a course of action we pursued with our communities foremost in our minds and, while I am disappointed at the outcome, I am pleased that we stood up for them in this way."

A spokesperson for Springwell Solar Farm said the company was pleased the legal challenge had been dismissed.

"Springwell Solar Farm will make important contributions to the UK's security of electricity supply and net zero goals," they said.

They added the farm would "create up to 600 jobs during the peak of construction, as well as introducing a community benefit fund for the lifetime of the project that will be used to support local communities and initiatives near to the site".

A DESNZ spokesperson said: "We welcome this decision. Solar is one of the cheapest and quickest forms of energy to build, helping get bills down for good."

The development is one of several large solar farms to be given permission in the county.

A separate legal challenge against the Beacon Fen Solar Farm. near Sleaford, was announced by Lincolnshire County Council last month.

articles.title: Yemen’s Houthis hold mass funeral as they call for action to protect civilians
articles.summary: A mass funeral procession was held in the Yemeni capital Sanaa on Wednesday for at least 43 people allegedly killed in an airstrike by the Saudi-led coalition, according to Saba news agency, which is run by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
articles.body: A mass funeral procession was held in the Yemeni capital Sanaa on Wednesday for at least 43 people allegedly killed in an airstrike by the Saudi-led coalition, according to Saba news agency, which is run by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The victims were killed in a strike Saturday on six homes in Al-Shariya, a Yemeni village east of Sanaa, Saba said. Among the dead are 21 children and 10 women, the agency reported. Footage aired on the Houthi-run Masirah TV showed large crowds gathered at a graveyard. Men carrying rifles were seen digging graves. Ahead of the funeral, Masirah TV published graphic images showing children lying motionless, whom Houthi authorities said had been killed in the strike. The attack involved three consecutive raids that also hit ambulance crews and rescue workers, it said. CNN has reached out to the Saudi government as well as the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen for comment. Fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition reignited in July, shattering a 2022 UN-brokered ceasefire that had brought years of relative calm, after Saudi-backed forces struck Sanaa Airport in an attempt to block a Houthi plane arriving from Iran. Houthi forces retaliated by launching an offensive and captured territory along Yemen’s western coast and near the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a key trade route. Saturday’s attack comes as casualties surge in Yemen, where the years long conflict has dragged the country into a severe humanitarian crisis. As of Tuesday, the total number of casualties in Yemen has reached 11,755 since October 31, including 2,098 deaths, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). The daily average has increased considerably this month, according to the WHO count. On Wednesday, Yemen’s Houthi-controlled parliament appealed to United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres to intervene amid the intensifying fighting. The parliament claimed that hundreds of Saudi airstrikes over the previous five days had killed or wounded more than 300 people, most of them children, women and elderly people. CNN hasn’t independently verified the figure. The Houthi-run Health Ministry also said Wednesday that at least 359 civilians had been killed and 780 wounded in what it described as the latest Saudi escalation. The ministry said most were women and children. The Houthi armed forces said Tuesday that Saudi Arabia had carried out 93 airstrikes and missile attacks over the previous 24 hours, targeting sites including civilian and energy infrastructure across Houthi-controlled areas. The rebel group, in turn, continues to target Saudi infrastructure, including the King Khalid International Airport in the capital Riyadh, and oil facilities. In October, back-to-back attacks on the airport killed at least 20 people and wounded hundreds of others. On Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted two drones over Mecca, Islam’s holiest city. On Thursday, it intercepted another over Riyadh. The Houthis denied targeting Mecca, calling the coalition’s claim “another lie.” Over the weekend, a building belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco in the financial district of Riyadh was damaged in a missile attack.

articles.title: Before Scott Colom, these two men were the last black US senators from Mississippi
articles.summary: The Democratic candidate won in a southern state that had not seated a black senator since 1874.
articles.body:
After winning a close race in Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom will become the state's first black US senator for more than 150 years, and the third in history.

It is a historic result in the deeply conservative southern state that last sent a Democrat to the US Senate in 1982, and had not seated a black senator since 1875.

Colom follows Hiram Revels, who became the first black person ever to serve in the chamber when he was seated from 1870 to 1871, and Blanche Bruce, whose term ran from 1875 to 1881. Revels and Bruce were both members of the Republican Party.

Revels was chosen as Mississippi's first senator after the Civil War, serving for just over a year and campaigning strongly for racial equality.

A few years later, Bruce, who was born into slavery, became the first black person to serve a full term in the US Senate. He remained in Washington after leaving the chamber and held a role in the Treasury.

Both terms came before the repressive Jim Crow laws began to enforce racial segregation across Mississippi and other southern US states.

A significant factor in Colom's victory was his success in mobilising young people and the state's large black population, who are expected to have turned out in high numbers.

In a victory speech, Colom referenced how Revels, who was a minister and served as a chaplain during the Civil War, gained support for his Senate campaign through his words.

"That's an example of the power of prayer, and through our history, there are so many people that lifted this state up through the power of prayer in very dark times," Colom said.

Prior to the result being called, the BBC spoke to students at Jackson State University, a historically black college in Mississippi. Many of them had voted for the first time and backed Colom.

"I really feel like a change is what we need," 18-year-old Jamyria Dunn said.

"I've had some amazing days in my life," she continued, "but seeing Mississippi, this state in particular, turn blue, would really bring a light to my heart that people just would not understand."

articles.title: Guernsey animal owners want more firework display restrictions
articles.summary: One sheep farmer says their animal was singed by what was thought to be firework rocket remnants.
articles.body:
Animal owners in Guernsey are calling for more restrictions around firework displays.

Displays were held across the island in early November to mark Budloe, bonfire or Guy Fawkes night, but some people said the unpredictability of private displays meant they were unable to prepare.

Denise Fallaize said a burn mark believed to be caused by rocket remnants was found on one of her sheep's fleece, while another animal owner, Sara Clarke, said the event was "absolutely horrendous" for her dog.

On the issue, Deputy Adrian Gabriel, President of the Committee for the Environment & Infrastructure, said: "We'll be reviewing our strategic priorities at the end of this year."

As part of the States' fireworks etiquette , it asks organisers to register any displays on its website and islanders can subscribe for notifications of events, but the system is voluntary and organisers do not have to register.

Fallaize said when her husband went to check on their flock on Friday he noticed singeing on the back of one of their sheep, named Lucky.

"The only explanation we can think of is that the remnants of a firework rocket had landed on her back and actually slowly singed her fleece," she said.

"Fortunately, not through to her skin. But even so, it could have been, I'm sure, a frightening experience for her."

She said another of their animals, a young ram called Napoleon, had bolted through an electric fence and became stuck in brambles and needed to be cut out.

"We just imagine there were fireworks in the area and he became distressed and did what sheep do which is to bolt without thinking about it," Fallaize said.

She said they currently had a number of ewes they hoped were pregnant and they were concerned as "stress can lead them to abort at this early stage".

Fallaize suggested restrictions to reduce the number of displays and allowing them on one day.

Clarke is the owner of two dogs - Bella and Tinkerbell - with the latter being "very reactive" to loud noises.

"She gets upset, she runs around barking, panting, she can't sleep, she doesn't eat," she said. "It's just horrifying watching her."

She said firework remnants had landed in both her front and back gardens, adding there had been "so many unregistered displays".

"There was several that were going off near to my house, the noise of them, the proximity, the fact that you're not expecting them means you can't prepare your dogs for them," she said.

"It takes days for these dogs to actually settle properly.

"I just feel that private displays need far more legislation around them."

Clarke said she would prefer displays to be limited to professionally organised public displays on certain days.

Gabriel said: "The ability to consider any changes to legislation will depend on various factors including prioritisation of existing workstreams and the States as a whole having the resources available."

Ben Hunter, who organised St Martin's AC football club display, said the events were a "financial boost" and a time for community to come together.

Hunter said the public display on 7 November was a way for the football club to raise money and bring the local community together.

He said it was an important fundraiser for lots of groups in the islands but added: "We can't do them all on the same night."

"I understand that we shouldn't be letting off fireworks for seven days," Hunter said.

He said he understood the importance of registering a display, but did not want to see too many limitations on events.

articles.title: Romanov sapphire bracelet smashes auction estimate, sells for $4.9 million
articles.summary: A bracelet containing a huge sapphire that used to be part of the Imperial Russian crown jewels has sold for almost $5 million, smashing its pre-auction estimate.
articles.body: A bracelet containing a huge sapphire that used to be part of the Imperial Russian crown jewels has sold for almost $5 million, smashing its pre-auction estimate. The cushion-shaped 197.80-carat Romanov sapphire is set in a geometric diamond bracelet by jeweler Cartier, according to a listing from auction house Sotheby’s, which sold the piece in Geneva, Switzerland, on Wednesday. The sale price of 4.1 million Swiss Francs ($4.9 million) means the bracelet smashed its pre-auction estimate of 850,000 to 1.7 million Swiss francs ($1.02 million to $2.04 million). “This exceptional historical sapphire originated in the legendary collection of the Romanov family,” reads the auction listing. “The fabled collection of the Russian Tsars was arguably the most opulent and valuable Royal collection ever assembled.” The Romanovs were the last Russian monarchy, and their rule ended in 1917 when Czar Nicholas II abdicated the throne at the beginning of the Russian Revolution. The following year, the family was executed by the Bolsheviks. It is not known exactly when the Romanovs acquired the sapphire, but it can be seen alongside its pair on the front panel of a skirt worn by the Dowager Empress Maria Feodorovna, Nicholas II’s mother, at a ball in 1883, according to the auction listing. Following the Russian Revolution, the Romanov collection was sold off by the Soviets in the 1920s, after which this sapphire was acquired by a socialite named Ganna Walska in 1927, said Sotheby’s. At the time it was mounted on a necklace, and by the time it was sold as part of Walska’s estate in 1971 it had been moved onto a different, shorter necklace, according to the auction house. In 2015, Cartier mounted the sapphire on the bracelet it is seen on today. “The bracelet, with interchangeable rock crystal centre, highlights both the historical Romanov sapphire as well as Cartier’s unique artistic legacy anchored in the art deco period,” according to Sotheby’s. Previous auctions of Romanov jewels have also fetched far more than their estimate. In 2021, a sapphire and diamond brooch and matching earrings sold for 806,500 Swiss francs (about $883,600) at Sotheby’s, almost twice the high-end of the pre-sale estimate.

articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Thursday that Ukrainian military units recorded disruptions to the Starshield ​satellite communications service for days.

The Ukrainian president said in a post on the social platform X that restrictions were limiting the speed at which Starshield could be used ​to 100 mph. As a result, Zelensky said, Ukrainian interceptors could not reach sufficient speed to down ​Russian jet-powered drones.

“This means more Russian strikes get through, and more of our people are killed by Russia,” Zelensky said. “We are trying to get the details from the American side, but so far, we know very little.”

This comes a day after Russia and Ukraine agreed to a “large-scale” exchange of prisoners of war followed by two days of U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi.

Ukraine faced a similar slowdown last month , which restricted its access to Starshield, the military version of Starlink.

Starlink services were cut off for objects that traveled more than 100 mph, impacting the capabilities of Ukraine’s drones, airplanes and helicopters.

The incident sparked questions about who was behind the decision to cause the slowdown.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk initially claimed that the choice to restrict the speed or usage of Starshield is made by the U.S. military and, ultimately, the president. He later alluded to being involved in the decision in a post on social media, writing, “Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week.”

Ukraine has used Starlink’s commercial services since the beginning of its war with Russia. It later added Starshield through SpaceX’s contract with the Pentagon. Musk noted in his post that Starlink is “critical to the defense of Ukraine.”

Trump administration officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, have previously said that the White House did not have anything to do with the slowdown.

Zelensky, in a recent interview with PBS News , expressed doubt that the SpaceX CEO could be the lone decisionmaker behind the initial slowdown.

“I’m not sure that he [Musk] can do it with Starshield because it’s military. It’s government version,” Zelensky said.

articles.title: 67+ Indigenous-owned brands to shop for the holidays and beyond
articles.summary: We rounded up a list of Indigenous-owned brands we think you should know about across food, jewelry, beauty and more.
articles.body: Mya Beaudry is 15 years old and already six years into owning her business, Kokom Scrunchies. Beaudry is Algonquin from Kitigan Zibi Anishinabeg First Nation, an identity she says is a big part of who she is and “at the heart of Kokom Scrunchies.” Beaudry’s mother, Marcie, taught her to sew at nine years old as a creative way to raise money and host Indigenous youth events in her community. She began making scrunchies from fabric inspired by the floral scarves commonly worn by kokoms, which means “grandmother” in Algonquin, says Beaudry. Indigenous peoples speak more than 4,000 of the world’s approximately 6,700 languages, but the United Nations estimates that one Indigenous language dies every two weeks. Many of the Indigenous business owners I spoke to say languages are central to Indigenous peoples’ identities, cultures and worldviews, and several on this list incorporate their cultures, traditions and communities into their work. Like Beaudry, many Indigenous business owners on this list draw inspiration from their Indigenous identities and traditions. In the United States, November is Native American Heritage Month, but you can support Indigenous-owned businesses year-round. According to the U.S. Small Business Administration’s Office of Advocacy, there were more than 400,000 Indigenous-owned businesses in the U.S. alone in 2021. I talked with more than 60 business owners about their Indigenous identity, biggest challenges and the inspiration behind their brands, and compiled a list of Indigenous-owned brands spanning the United States, Canada, Australia and Latin America that we think you should know about. For its business statistics, the Census Bureau defines ownership as having at least 51% of the stock or equity in a business, and its racial ownership categories include American Indian or Alaska Native businesses. For this story, I used that majority-ownership definition and confirmed with each brand that it’s at least 51% Indigenous-owned. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. Indigenous-owned beauty and wellness brands Cheekbone Beauty A vivid dream of young Indigenous girls dolled up with colorful lip glosses is what led Anishinaabe founder Jenn Harper to launch Cheekbone Beauty, which offers lipstick, eyeshadow, blush and other makeup products. Harper’s goal was to create a beauty brand where Indigenous shoppers could see themselves represented. Cheekbone is also a part of the PACT Mail Back Program, where customers can ship empty products like lipstick and highlighter back to Cheekbone to be properly recycled. N8iV Beauty Ruth-Ann Thorn, who is Payómkawichum and Luiseño, was shopping at Sephora with her daughter when she realized the lack of Indigenous representation in beauty. “We were standing in a store filled with beauty brands, on our own ancestral continent, and I couldn’t point to a brand that represented our people,” she says. “I wanted my daughter to see that we belong in those spaces and that [our] knowledge [of plants and nature] has value.” This inspired Thorn to create N8iV, offering serums, cleansers and more. Sisters Sage In 2018, founder Lynn-Marie Angus was working in high-rise construction, facing a great deal of racism and sexism from colleagues, according to Angus. Her sister was pregnant and at risk of becoming homeless, so they came together to create Sisters Sage, a wellness brand making soaps, smokeless smudge sprays and other bath, body and wellness products to embrace the sisters’ Indigenous Gitxaała, Nisga’a and Métis cultures and traditions.. Sister Sky Sister Sky was founded 27 years ago by sisters Monica Simeon and Marina TurningRobe, members of the Spokane Tribe of Indians. They have mixed texture hair and struggled to find products that worked, inspiring them to create hair care designed for a variety of textures. “There was a whole community of women whose hair care needs weren’t being met,” says Simeon. They’ve spent over two decades growing their company and say the biggest challenge is finding what makes the products special to others. “Over the years, we’ve learned that you don’t have to appeal to everyone. What matters is being genuine about what you offer and building a community of customers and partners who truly value it,” Simeon and TurningRobe told me in a joint email. Through these challenges, the sisters say their heritage has kept them grounded. “One of the greatest lessons our culture has taught us is the importance of community. We’re all part of something bigger than ourselves.” Sister Sky offers a variety of hair products, including shampoo, conditioner, hair mist, detangler and hair brushes. Skwálwen Botanicals Dr. Leigh Joseph is an ethnobotanist and researcher from the Squamish Nation who turned to Indigenous plant science to formulate skin care products, including cleansers, face creams and bath salts. Products incorporate plants like wild rose, devil’s club, stinging nettle and sage. Indigenous-owned clothing and accessories brands Awasis Boutique Christine Marie founded Awasis, a Cree word meaning “child,” while she was a stay-at-home mother to her two children. Marie began sewing bibs and aprons while caring for her children, a passion project that grew into a line of onesies, t-shirts and blankets for newborns, toddlers and children four years and older. Awasis also carries select t-shirts in adult sizes. Ginew Ginew originated from co-founders Erik Brodt and Amanda Bruegl’s wedding ceremony. “My father shot a buffalo for the wedding and we prepared the hide from the buffalo in the garage,” says Brodt. Then, the couple made the hide into belts as a meaningful gift to those who helped with the ceremony. During a trip to West Texas, Brodt began thinking about the clothing people needed as their work shifted from hunting to agriculture. “The Heritage Coat, our first apparel item, [was born] on a napkin in the common space at El Cosmico,” says Brodt. Ginew sells denim jackets inspired by the founders’ Oneida, Stockbridge-Munsee Mohican and Ojibwe ancestry, along with shirts, patches and bandanas. Kené Kaya Kené Kaya is a fashion house owned by Alessandra Durand, who is of Quechua heritage. The brand is based in Peru, and while Quechua-owned, also works closely with women artists from the Shipibo-Conibo tribe of the Peruvian Amazon. Collaborating across Indigenous groups is exactly “what makes [them] unique,” says Durand. Kené Kaya’s products, which include shirts, dresses and accessories, are hand-embroidered and painted by Shipibo-Conibo women and made of fabrics like Peruvian cotton. Kokom Scrunchies Each scrunchie designed by Mya Beaudry is named after an Indigenous figure or family member (for example, Kokom Lola is named after Beaudry’s grandmother). “It’s a way to celebrate the people who have helped shape who I am and remind other young girls that they can be role models and leaders too,” she says. Beaudry says her scrunchies are now sold in more than 150 stores across Canada. “Being Indigenous means being proud of where I come from,” she says. 4Kinship 4Kinship founder Amy Denet Deal was adopted at birth. After reconnecting with her Diné heritage, she began using her business to help create economic opportunities in her community, like the Diné Skate Garden Project, a center for Indigenous youth. 4Kinship sells vintage clothing and original pieces using upcycled materials, homeware, jewelry, art and books. Indigenous-owned jewelry brands Beyond Buckskin Beyond Buckskin was founded in 2009 by Jessica Metcalfe of the Turtle Mountain Chippewa tribe and offers apparel, accessories, blankets and more. Based in North Dakota, the brand partners with more than 40 Indigenous artists to bring their work to a broader audience. Haus of Dizzy Founder Kristy Dickenson uses unique materials and designs, like mirrored acrylic, glitter, bold patterns and the Aboriginal flag, in her jewelry and accessories. “I’ve always loved fashion, color, music and making a statement,” she says. “Growing up as a proud Wiradjuri woman, I also understood the importance of identity, representation and being unapologetically yourself.” Her range of products includes t-shirts, earrings and hair accessories featuring activist and political messages. “Activism doesn’t always have to be serious or confronting,” she says. “It can be joyful, colourful, funny and full of love. That’s what I try to bring to my designs.” Running Fox Beads When owner Skye Paul visited Beauval, Saskatchewan, at 15 years old, she hesitated to help butcher a moose. Instead, her aunt taught her how to bead, giving her another way to connect with her culture. Now, she beads tattoo-flash-inspired designs including Dene floral motifs onto moose hide, and fashions them into earrings. Sapling and Flint Sisters Dakota and Jesse Brant founded Sapling and Flint in 2017 as a way to immerse their growing families in the Mohawk Turtle Clan culture in Ontario. “I am proud to have a business here in my community where I can raise my son in our culture while being able to share with others about who we are as Mohawk people,” says Dakota. With Jesse’s background in jewelry making and Dakota’s business experience, they work together to create earrings, rings and pendants inspired by their culture, family and connections to Turtle Island. Indigenous-owned home and kitchen brands Eighth Generation Based in Seattle, Washington, Eighth Generation is owned by the Snoqualmie Tribe and strives to be an ethical alternative to inauthentic “Native-inspired” designs, according to the brand. Its tagline, “Inspired Natives, not Native-inspired,” reflects that mission. The brand offers blankets, candles, gifts and more. Mahota Textiles Textile designer Margaret Roach Wheeler started Mahota Textiles in 1984, named after her great-great-great grandmother, who came to Indian Territory (present-day south-central Oklahoma) during the 1844 Chickasaw removal. Wheeler makes blankets, pillows and table runners inspired by Chickasaw and Southeastern textile traditions to honor the five generations of Chickasaw women in her family. Onquata Mother-daughter duo Lise and Lara Siouï founded the French-Canadian brand Onquata (Lara’s Wendat name) in 2018 with a range of painted paddles designed for home display or use on the water. The brand has since expanded to include home goods, accessories and wellness products. Rashelle Nêhiyaw designer Rashelle Campbell was always interested in interior design, but it wasn’t until the Covid-19 pandemic that she leaned into it, making maximalist tufted rugs. Campbell says running the business requires her to wear several hats, and that she once felt pressure to say yes to every opportunity, even when it meant overworking herself. “I felt like I had to say yes to every opportunity because, as an Indigenous woman, we don’t receive as many opportunities as others,” she says. Campbell’s work is heavily inspired by early-2000s pop culture and colorful nostalgia. “So much of our story is told through sorrow and resilience,” she says. “And while those stories are important, I think we need to talk more about our joy, too.” Totem Design House Totem Design House is a family-run business on the K’omoks First Nation territory of Vancouver Island, British Columbia. “Unlike most Indigenous brands that specialize in one or two product categories, we’ve built an incredibly diverse collection,” says founder Erin Brillon, who is a member of the Laana Tsadas Eagle Clan of Skidegate Haida. “Approximately 80% of everything we sell is produced in-house at our Vancouver Island studios.” These products include jewelry, blankets, art, apparel, candles and skincare. Brillon also hosts the podcast “Together We Rise,” which features Indigenous women sharing their stories. Indigenous-owned bookstores and art Beam Paints Anong Beam grew up in a world of color, raised by artist parents who taught her how to harvest pigment on Manitoulin Island. “I was really lucky to be raised close to them, they travelled a lot and I was homeschooled for most of elementary school,” says Beam. “That early education became the cornerstone of my business.” After her father passed away in 2005, Beam began experimenting with making paint, and officially launched Beam Paints on her father’s birthday 12 years later. The brand sells watercolor paints made with pigments, gum arabic and maple sap. “We make everything here from raw materials; we crush rocks and we gather sap from our family’s maple sugar bush here on Manitoulin island,” she says. Beam Paints also has a Paint Club program, which lets you receive a monthly selection of paints, paintable cards and designs. Birchbark Books Birchbark Books is an independent bookstore in Minnesota, owned by Louise Erdrich of the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa. It stocks both books by Indigenous authors and Indigenous-focused books, and hosts local readings for the community. Its online store also has an extensive selection of children’s books by and about Indigenous people. Saretta Art & Design Owned and operated in the Hunter Valley of New South Wales, Australia, Saretta Art & Design is run by Saretta Fielding, who is a Wonnarua woman of the Upper Hunter Valley through her grandmother and an Anaiwan woman of the New England area through her grandfather. She makes sand art, inspired by traditional engravings of the Wonnarua Country. Strong Nations Strong Nations is an Indigenous-owned bookstore on the Snuneymuxw First Nation territory in Canada that specializes in publishing educational resources, including thousands of works by Indigenous authors and illustrators. It also offers translation packages for many of its books to help boost language revitalization in the community. The Farmer’s Daughter Fibers Candice English grew up in northwest Montana connected to her mother’s Blackfeet heritage and her father’s sheep ranch. During what she calls her “midlife crisis,” English began dyeing yarn, and now sells more than 70 yarn varieties. articles.title: The risk of blindness from GLP-1 drugs is too serious to ignore
articles.summary: When a medication is prescribed to millions of people, even an uncommon complication can affect a substantial number of individuals.
articles.body:
The popularity of GLP-1 medications has transformed the treatment of obesity and diabetes. Drugs such as Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro and Zepbound have offered millions of people a new approach to managing obesity.

There is, however, a risk of blindness with these drugs that is everyone using them must be aware of.

This week, the Food and Drug Administration finally required manufacturers of GLP-1 medications to include warnings about a potentially serious eye condition called non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. Europe recognized the warning before the U.S. did. The decision follows an earlier determination by European regulators that this should be classified as a very rare potential side effect of semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy .

The FDA’s decision is an important step, but patients and physicians should not mistake a warning on a drug label for an adequate response to a potentially devastating complication.

I have spent much of my professional career studying the relationship between vision, the optic nerve and systemic disease. Nearly three decades ago, I studied this eye condition and published a landmark paper on it. What has remained troubling throughout my work is how little we know about precisely why it happens and, more importantly, how little we can do to remedy it once it does.

The condition is sometimes described as a stroke of the optic nerve. It occurs when blood flow to the front portion of the optic nerve is compromised, depriving the nerve tissue of the oxygen and nutrients it needs to function. Unlike many conditions that gradually affect eyesight, it can announce itself quite suddenly. A person may wake up one morning and discover that vision in one eye has become blurred, distorted or substantially diminished. There may be no pain or warning that anything is wrong.

The consequences can be permanent. There is currently no established treatment that reliably restores vision lost to this condition. Although some patients experience limited spontaneous improvement, many are left with lasting visual impairment. For someone who drives, works, reads or depends on vision for everyday independence, the consequences extend far beyond the eye itself.

This is what makes the emerging association between GLP-1 medications and non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy so important. The concern is not that everyone taking these medications will develop blindness. This condition is rare, and the scientific evidence has not established a definitive cause-and-effect relationship with GLP-1 drugs. When a medication is prescribed to millions of people, even an uncommon complication can affect a substantial number of individuals.

The European Medicines Agency concluded in 2025 that non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy should be recognized as a very rare adverse effect of semaglutide, potentially affecting up to 1 in 10,000 users . The FDA has now conducted its own extensive review, including clinical trial data involving more than 134,000 participants. Its analysis found 6.4 cases of per 100,000 among GLP-1 users.

There is another complication that makes this issue particularly difficult for patients and physicians. Many people taking GLP-1 medications also have diabetes, an established independent risk factor for the same condition.

Diabetes can independently damage vision through diabetic retinopathy , a condition affecting the blood vessels of the retina. It can also increase the risk of optic nerve ischemia. Consequently, when someone taking a GLP-1 medication experiences a change in vision, distinguishing between an underlying diabetic complication and a possible medication-associated event is not always straightforward.

Patients should not be expected to make that distinction themselves. Nor should they have to wait until they experience sudden vision loss to discover that an ophthalmologic evaluation might have been useful.

This is why I believe eye care needs to become a more integral part of the conversation surrounding GLP-1 prescribing. Patients should receive a comprehensive eye examination when starting these medications, including an assessment of optic nerve health and a review of existing retinal disease.

For patients with diabetes, this should complement, not replace, their established diabetic eye screening. A baseline examination provides an opportunity to identify preexisting conditions, document optic nerve anatomy and establish a reference point should visual symptoms develop.

Anyone taking these medications should know that sudden, painless loss of vision in either eye, new blind spots, missing portions of the visual field or unexplained visual distortion requires immediate medical attention. These symptoms should never be attributed casually to fatigue, aging or diabetes. Patients should contact their physician immediately and obtain urgent ophthalmologic evaluation.

The pharmaceutical industry, regulators and prescribing physicians have a responsibility to ensure that patients understand what they are taking and what warning signs they should recognize.

In medicine, we often focus on treating disease once it becomes apparent. This blinding condition presents a different challenge. By the time the patient recognizes the problem, the damage may be irreversible. We cannot promise to restore what has been lost, and we do not yet fully understand why it happens.

That is precisely why we need to take this warning seriously. Saving someone’s vision should be as important as improving their metabolic health. A medication that helps people live longer and healthier lives should never come at the expense of failing to protect one of their most fundamental senses.

Sreedhar Potarazu, MD, MBA, is an author, board-certified ophthalmologist and clinical director at American Eye Care.
