articles.title: Trump: ‘Huge CARAVANS are … beginning illegal march through Mexico’
articles.summary: President Trump on Thursday reacted to reports that more than 1,000 migrants are heading toward the U.S. from Mexico, which he connected to sweeping Republican losses in the midterms. A Chiapas state government source told Reuters that around 1,500 people, including several families with small children and strollers, left the Mexican city of Tapachula by…
articles.body:
President Trump on Thursday reacted to reports that more than 1,000 migrants are heading toward the U.S. from Mexico, which he connected to sweeping Republican losses in the midterms.

A Chiapas state government source told Reuters that around 1,500 people, including several families with small children and strollers, left the Mexican city of Tapachula by Guatemala’s border on Tuesday.

“Here we go again! With the perceived loss by the Republicans in the Midterms — I WAS NOT ON THE BALLOT — the INVASION of our Country is taking place again,” Trump wrote on Truth Social . “Huge CARAVANS are forming and beginning their illegal march through Mexico.”

He directed a warning toward Mexico, saying the country’s government must stop the caravan or the “Tariffs on Mexico will be IMMEDIATELY DOUBLED.”

“MEXICO, THE GOVERNOR OF TEXAS, THE VERY LIBERAL NEW GOVERNOR OF TEXAS, OUR GREAT BORDER PATROL, & ICE, HAVE BEEN SO INFORMED,” the president’s post concluded. “There will be no leniency!”

Many of the migrants, coming from Central America, told Reuters and other outlets that the Democratic victories last week could open new opportunities for them in the U.S.

“There might be a light at the end of the tunnel, a way for us to ​get in,” Cesar Sandoval, a 47-year-old Nicaraguan migrant who the U.S. deported a few months ago, told the outlet. “We believe the Democrats will help us … with God’s help.”

They are looking to reach Mexico City to receive help from the federal government and protection against detainment at the U.S. border, according to Reuters.

Honduran migrant Billy Noe Martinez, who survived the 2010 massacre of 72 migrants in Tamaulipas, said he hoped Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum would be moved by the their situation “and allow us to move forward,” the newswire reported.

Trump made migrant caravans a key message ahead of the 2018 midterms with unfounded claims that Democrats were seemingly behind the movement. The president even claimed that there were Middle Eastern migrants and terrorists mixed in with the groups, before admitting to a reporter that there was “no proof of anything” when asked about the rhetoric.

This messaging was mirrored prior to the 2026 midterms amid student protests across Europe, notably in France.

Trump, Vice President Vance and other administration officials as well as Republican lawmakers claimed immigrants from Muslim-majority countries were behind the protests and clashes with police, even as reports cited students protesting for better school conditions and lodging .

Following last week’s elections, Trump said his deportation crackdown since returning to the presidency might have been “ too tough ” and likely contributed to the GOP’s losses . The replacement of Susie Wiles with longtime adviser Stephen Miller, a hard-liner on immigration , as White House chief of staff signals a different message.

articles.title: In 1996, Eddie Van Halen gave Jason Becker a guitar with a promise that they would play together; 27 years later, Becker auctioned it for $110,000 to finance his ongoing treatment
articles.summary: In a remarkable story of friendship and legacy, Jason Becker auctions off the iconic guitar gifted to him by Eddie Van Halen for $110,000 to aid in his ALS treatment. Discover the emotional journey behind this historic instrument.
articles.body: When talking about guitar legends, most would agree on the stature of Eddie Van Halen as a legendary guitarist. But only a few would remember Jason Becker or speak of him in the same revered tone. According to Guernsey’s auction, Becker’s career was a case of quick-burn stardom after he exploded on the rock scene in the mid-1980s at age 16. By the time he was 20, his playing days would dwindle after contracting ALS.The inscription on the black Peavey EVH Wolfgang guitar carried a promise that its recipient could not know whether he would be able to fulfil it, Guernsey’s auction noted. Van Halen had written it for Becker after visiting the young guitarist at his Southern California home on 31 August 1996.Eventually, the guitar went under the hammer at Guernsey’s auction house in New York for $110,000, Guitar World reported in 2023. Becker had put the instrument up for sale to finance his ongoing treatment, and the final bid fell short of the pre-estimate of $300,000 to $400,000.A gift sealed with a thumbprintVan Halen’s visit to Becker took place after the latter had been diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, aka ALS, in 1989. Van Halen travelled to his home as a sign of support, and the whole visit was filmed for an ALS awareness video. During the meeting, Van Halen played part of “Eruption” and other pieces on the guitar before handing it over to Becker. The meeting was concluded with a handwritten dedication by Van Halen, which read: “Jason. We will play guitar together in the future. Love, from the heart to your soul. Eddie Van Halen, 96”. The guitar also bore Becker’s thumbprint on the back of the neck.The guitar came from the first 100 Peavey EVH Wolfgang models produced, and it was numbered #69. Van Halen himself had tested the guitars and selected a few of them for personal use. The one given to Becker was checked and set up by Jim DeCola, Peavey’s guitar design engineer and the Wolfgang’s designer.The Wolfgang was named after Van Halen’s son. At the time, production of signature models was a recent trend. Its features included Van Halen’s D-Tune system fitted to the Floyd Rose tremolo, according to Guitar World. The guitar came with its original certificate of authenticity.Letting go of history and moving onBecker had already sold three instruments that he himself played through an earlier Guernsey’s auction. In 2023, he decided to part ways with the Van Halen guitar. It had been hanging on his wall rather than being played, and he was comfortable with another owner taking responsibility for it.According to Guitar World, Becker would indulge visitors to his home who would often recognise the guitar’s connection to Van Halen. His family would tell them about the afternoon when Van Halen visited, sat with them and played guitar together. Becker spoke of Van Halen’s generosity not only to him but to his family, and of how their friendship endured until the latter died in 2020.Although Becker could no longer play the guitar, walk or speak by 2023, he continued to compose music, relying on a communication system developed with his father. Using eye movements, he selected letters and musical information while his team transferred his ideas into computer software and prepared parts for musicians.As a teenager in California, Becker had recorded two albums with Marty Friedman as part of Cacophony. He released the solo record “Perpetual Burn” in 1988 and later joined David Lee Roth’s band and recorded as Roth’s guitarist on the 1991 album “A Little Ain’t Enough”.Becker released “Triumphant Hearts” in December 2018. The album featured performances by guitarists and musicians including Joe Satriani, Steve Vai, Neal Schon, Steve Morse, Paul Gilbert and Joe Bonamassa. Guitar World also reported in 2023 that Becker had discussed a subsequent project called “The Strawberry Jams”.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Rescuer admits defeat in battle to keep Harriet the badger
articles.summary: Graeme Wilson says the animal he rescued is in a new licensed home to live a "long, happy life".
articles.body:
An ecologist from the Borders has admitted defeat in his battle to be allowed to keep a badger he nursed back to health after she was found in a cattle trough.

Graeme Wilson, who runs a small wildlife rehabilitation service at his home in Denholm, had an application to keep the animal - named Harriet - rejected by NatureScot.

His bid to keep the badger was then strongly criticised by three animal welfare charities.

Wilson said Harriet had been moved to a new home which was licensed to keep her and he was going to take a break from wildlife rescue.

Badger rescuer criticised by wildlife welfare charities

Man fighting for custody of badger he nursed back from starvation

He was called out to help the badger when she was found in the trough about 300ft (100m) from her sett.

He believes she had been hand-reared prior to this and would not survive in the wild.

He applied to NatureScot to be allowed to keep Harriet using an educational licence, but it turned the application down.

Then the British Wildlife Rehabilitation Council, Scottish Badgers and the Badgers Trust issued a statement criticising his actions and saying they raised serious animal welfare concerns.

The BWRC, which works in wildlife casualty welfare in the UK, said it had suspended Wilson's membership as he had not upheld its principles.

It opposes the permanent captivity of any native British wild animal and said they should be humanely euthanised in all but exceptional circumstances if they cannot return to the wild.

Wilson told BBC Scotland News he had given up his fight to keep Harriet and she had now been moved to a licensed home.

"I always said, I'd be delighted if Harriet could stay with me, but I'd be heartbroken if she had to go," he said.

"However, I just wanted her safe and that was all this was about.

"She is now somewhere safe and free from the threat of being forced into release where she was likely to die or euthanasia or going to a zoo where she was going to be stressed out - none of them are going to happen now.

"She's going to have a long, happy life."

He confirmed he intended to take a "wee break" from wildlife rescue following the statement by wildlife organisations which he said had led to some people approaching him and a colleague with "very nasty" comments.

He stressed that from the outset he had liaised with others including vets, badger groups and other rehabbers and Harriet's care had been based on those discussions.

Scottish Badgers said it understood why so many people had been moved by the story of the badger at the centre of a "difficult and emotional debate about her future".

"Nobody wants Harriet to suffer," it said.

"Like everyone we want this badger to live, and above all to live the best life that is possible for her now.

"The challenge now that she is in some form of sheltered environment is to look to her future and to understand what arrangements can best and genuinely fulfil her range of needs."

It added the case showed there were lessons to be learned in terms of responsibilities to co-ordinate action from the earliest stage when "challenging situations" like this one came long.

The Badger Trust says that if you find an injured or unwell badger, contact a reputable and experienced wildlife rescue centre, a local badger group, the RSPCA or the Scottish SPCA for support.

A cub seen alone is not necessarily orphaned, so seek advice before intervening. If it is safe to do so, keep your distance, note where you found it and what you observed, and keep people and dogs away.

Do not feed it, move it, take it home or handle it. Let experienced rescuers advise on what to do next.

articles.summary: Jacob Fowler's .925 save percentage faces Jeremy Swayman's .920 mark as the Montreal Canadiens visit the Boston Bruins in a premier goalie duel.
articles.body: I was able to grab us a victory on the ice last night, and I'm hopeful we can do it again tonight. I don't love the NBA card all that much, and I've shared a play for the NFL already, so let's stick with hockey until I go up in flames and need to take a break from that. Their team has done a decent job on offense, scoring 3.33 goals per game, but they are allowing 3.06 per game as well. Perhaps that could be considered impressive because they have allowed more shots per game than they've taken. Montreal is solid enough to capitalize on Power Plays and is also adept at killing their opponents' power plays. Tonight, we will have Jacob Fowler in the net. Fowler is just 21 years old, but he has put together a fantastic second season so far. With Fowler in the net, he is 8-1-2 for the year, tied for the seventh-most wins in the league. He is allowing just 2.14 goals against per game, also the seventh-best in the league. His two shutouts rank second, and his save percentage is .925, good for third in the league. In other words, Fowler has been outstanding and one of the best goalies in hockey. He has been spectacular on the road, allowing just four goals in four games. MONTREAL CANADIENS MAKE WRONG KIND OF HISTORY WITH FOUR-GOAL CHOKE JOB ALMOST TOO SHOCKING TO BELIEVE The Boston Bruins are one of the best teams in hockey as well. This year, they are 13-4-1 for the season, and they have a stellar home record of 8-1-0. The Bruins' offense has been fantastic. They are putting almost four goals per game in the net. They are averaging 3.72 goals per game and have scored four or more goals in three of the past four wins. They are in great form as well, having won their past four games, including three of those at home. Even better is their defense. They are allowing just 2.28 goals per game to opponents. Tonight, they've confirmed that they will put Jeremy Swayman in the pipes. Like his counterpart, Swayman has put together a very strong early-season campaign. He is older than Fowler, but his numbers are about in line. Swayman is 9-3-1 for the year, putting him fourth in wins. articles.title: ‘Her hands are as cold as ice’: Gaza families struggle to keep warm
articles.summary: Flooded tents and high prices leave Gaza families struggling to keep children warm as winter approaches.
articles.body:
Gaza City, Gaza Strip – At night, as temperatures drop inside their makeshift shelter in Gaza City, Amira Saad struggles to keep her four-month-old baby, Mohammed, warm.

The baby mostly only has thin summer clothes. Unable to afford winter clothing, 27-year-old Amira has borrowed a warm garment from a neighbour, but remains worried about the cold during the night.

She lives with 18 family members, including nine children, under a tarp offering little protection from the elements. Finding enough warm clothes and blankets for everyone has become increasingly difficult.

The family was displaced from Gaza City’s Shujayea neighbourhood earlier in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, and now lives in a makeshift camp west of the city.

Recent heavy rain has flooded their shelter, soaking mattresses, pillows, and blankets.

“We were flooded while we were sleeping. The water came inside and soaked our blankets, mattresses and pillows. Everything was wet,” Amira says.

The children mostly have old, torn summer clothes. Amira’s mother-in-law, 60-year-old Basima Saad, is also worried about her own 23-year-old daughter, who has a disability, and needs warm clothes and medication.

“Her hands become as cold as ice. I keep her beside me in bed to warm her, just as I would a small child,” Basima says. “I dress her before I dress myself. I have to make sure she is warm first.”

With no regular income, the family relies on community kitchens for food. Spare money for winter clothes and blankets simply is not available.

“My husband does not have a job. Two days ago, he went out to work breaking up rubble, but he broke his hand. The situation is very bad, and the cold is extremely severe,” Amira says.

The danger to the Palestinians living in these conditions, and particularly the very young, is not hypothetical.

On Thursday, a nine-month-old baby, Kinan Ahmed Raqiq, died of hypothermia. His father told AFP that he woke up in his tent to find that his son’s skin had turned blue.

Tragedies like that make Amal al-Maydana, a 46-year-old other of seven, fearful.

She’s raising her children alone – her husband Hamza was killed by an Israeli quadcopter in January 2025, and her eldest son Haitham was killed by a sniper in November of the same year, age 25 at the time.

She is originally from Gaza City’s Zeitoun neighbourhood and has been displaced six times during the war, fleeing Israeli attacks and losing the family’s home, land, and car.

Now living in a tent, Amal struggles to provide for her children. Her younger daughters, Rimas and Malak, are still wearing summer clothes despite the arrival of winter .

“Everything is expensive… children’s clothes, shoes, everything,” she says.

Amal tries to make do with what is available, but it is not enough to meet her daughters’ needs.

Rain also seeps through the damaged tarpaulins covering the family’s tent. With no heating equipment, they rely on blankets to keep warm.

“We have no means of heating ourselves; we just cover the children with blankets,” she says.

Amal fears another storm will bring more rain and cold. “We just pray that God makes this winter easier for the people living in tents,” she says.

The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) says 94 percent of Gaza’s population urgently needs shelter assistance. Some 65 percent of households live in tents or makeshift shelters, while 650,000 children need winter aid, including warm clothing and blankets.

By September, aid agencies had secured enough winter clothing for just 9,000 households and bedding for 50,000 – far short of what was needed. OCHA said funding shortages were further hampering preparations for winter.

The UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) has warned that winter conditions put children in Gaza at increased risk of hypothermia and respiratory infections – at least 11 children died from hypothermia last winter, according to the Gaza Ministry of Health. The agency is seeking $97.5m for its 2026-2027 winter response, which aims to support 540,000 children and their families across Gaza and the occupied West Bank.

Recent rains have worsened the crisis. UNICEF said on November 9 that flooding had affected more than 106,000 people, while some 950,000 displaced Palestinians were living in flood-prone areas.

More than three years into Israel’s genocidal war, which has killed more than 74,600 Palestinians and wounded over 176,000, homes and livelihoods across Gaza have been devastated. Nearly two million people have been displaced, many repeatedly, and hundreds of thousands remain in tents and damaged shelters.

As the war enters its fourth year, unemployment and rising prices have made basic necessities increasingly unaffordable, leaving families struggling to protect their children from the cold.

Second-hand clothes and impossible choices

In Gaza City’s Rimal market, 25-year-old shop owner Mohammed Abu Shanar sees the same struggle among his customers. Many ask about winter clothing prices, but leave without buying anything.

“The prices are very high. They are not within everyone’s reach. People come in, ask how much something costs, and then leave because they cannot afford it,” he says.

Mohammed sells around four to six winter tracksuits a day. He says many children from nearby displacement camps still wear short-sleeved or lightweight clothes despite the cold.

He attributes the high prices to shortages of goods entering Gaza – the result of continued Israeli restrictions – and the cost of buying stock from wholesalers.

“First, there is a shortage of goods. The wholesalers hold on to their prices, and the merchandise is expensive for us, too. If these items were selling for 20 shekels ($6.25) or 25 shekels ($7.80) instead of 40 shekels ($12.60) or 50 shekels ($15.70), perhaps people would be able to buy them,” he says.

Mohammed says he has invested more than 20,000 shekels (about $6,265) in winter stock, but after three weeks of sales he has recovered less than 5,000 shekels (about $1,570).

People like Anas Hamad simply don’t have the money to buy from traders like Mohammed.

Anas and his family are displaced from Beit Hanoun in northern Gaza. Before the war, he ran a supermarket employing his four brothers. The war destroyed their homes and business, leaving all five university graduates without work.

With no income and unable to afford new clothes, Anas relies on second-hand markets and hand-me-downs to dress his three children.

He recalls how his five-year-old daughter, Jana, asked him for a new shirt. He could only point to the one she was wearing, which had belonged to her brother.

The family has lived in their badly torn tent for around two years. Despite his wife’s efforts to sew and patch it, rainwater enters from above and below. During the recent downpour, their bedding and belongings were soaked.

Anas says his three-year-old child was trembling from the cold, while the sound of rain hitting the tent frightened the children.

“I have to choose between buying food for my children, getting them warm clothes and blankets, or buying tarpaulins to protect our tent from the coming rain,” he says. “I don’t know what to prioritise or what to leave behind.”

articles.title: 2 children among the 8 dead in New York City building collapse, officials say
articles.summary: Two children were among the eight people killed after a New York City apartment building collapsed, officials said Thursday, as rescuers fought the rain in their continued, frantic search for possible survivors.
articles.body: Two children were among the eight people killed after a New York City apartment building collapsed, officials said Thursday, as rescuers fought the rain in their continued, frantic search for possible survivors. The FDNY crews were still in rescue mode more than 20 hours after the horrific collapse at 1321 Flatbush Ave. in Brooklyn, the city’s most populous borough. “We will be here until we are 100% sure there are no more people trapped,” FDNY Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore told reporters. “To be clear, we have not shifted from rescue to recovery. We are still in the search-and-rescue phase.” Six of the eight killed were pronounced dead at the scene, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. Two others died at the hospital. Before meeting with reporters at the scene, Mamdani said he visited victims recovering at the hospital. “This has been a very dark evening and morning for our city,” he said. “We are mourning too many people who we loved, and as we grieve and as we rebuild, we will do so together as one city.” The half-dozen dead adults also included a pair of construction workers, according to the mayor. There were 18 people injured, four of those were firefighters and 14 were civilians. One of those injured was listed in critical condition. “This is a devastating tragedy for New York and our prayers are with those who are recovering in the hospital and those who have died,” Bonsignore said. “The FDNY mourns with those families and we promise, with everything we have, we will not stop working until everyone is rescued or recovered.” The three-story apartment building came down at about 4 p.m. EST Wednesday, triggering a massive response from firefighters and other rescuers. Rescuers will be using heavier excavation equipment on Thursday that should be able to locate more bodies or survivors, officials said. “We we always assume that there are more people there until we can access the ground,” Bonsignore said. “So until we’ve removed some of the bigger, bigger debris and are able to search beneath them, this will remain a rescue operation.” The steady rain that pelted New York City on Thursday could slow rescue efforts but Bonsignore insisted that crews will fight through this challenge. “We are in the middle of a rainstorm but that will not stop our operations here,” she said. “It will definitely hinder our efforts. But this type of an emergency is something our members train extensively for.” The collapsed building, with a business on the ground floor and two stories of residential units above, was next to an excavation site where single-floor building had been cleared. “We will find out what happened and we will share that information with New Yorkers,” Mamdani said. There were “five main entities,” connected to that excavation project with crews from those companies working at about 100 construction sites around New York City, Mamdani said. “Our Department of Buildings is commencing sweeps of those sites today,” Mamdani said. The ongoing search also impacted neighboring residences with “water mains” shut down to 100 nearby buildings “so emergency crews can continue search and rescue operations,” according to a New York City Environment Protection statement on Thursday. It wasn’t immediately clear what caused the collapse but investigators will likely pay equal attention to the fallen building and the excavation site next door. Owners of that emptied property had been cleared to dig a maximum of 14 feet down, according to a building application.

articles.title: No plans to remove Walliams books from libraries in the West
articles.summary: The author and actor denies allegations of sexual misconduct and abuse of power.
articles.body:
Councils in the west have confirmed that books written by David Walliams will not be removed from libraries and schools.

Bristol, Gloucestershire, and Somerset are among council that have said they would not remove works by the author, who denies allegations of sexual misconduct and abuse of power.

Bristol and Somerset's libraries are overseen by LibrariesWest, whose guidance encourages libraries "to make available the broadest range of material" and "would only restrict access to material to protect it from damage or theft, not as a form of censorship". Gloucestershire operates a similar policy.

It is ultimately up to schools to decide if they want to remove books.

LibrariesWest also oversees libraries in Bath and North East Somerset (BANES), South Gloucestershire, North Somerset and several in Dorset.

A section in a document covering 'censorship and controversial stock' includes guidance from the Chartered Institute of Library and Information Professionals that librarians have a 'core and ongoing commitment to freedom of expression and freedom of access to information'.

The policy also says that "LibrariesWest will make available the broadest range of material within its policy of freedom of access to all legally available information.

It is acknowledged that on occasion individuals may find items in LibrariesWest libraries offensive.

However, we do not label items to warn customers of potentially sensitive content and would only restrict access to material to protect it from damage or theft, not as a form of censorship."

David Walliams sold around 50 million copies of his award winning children's books, which include titles like Gangsta Granny and Demon Dentist.

The actor and comedian was dropped by his publishers, Harper Collins, in 2025 over allegations around his conduct.

In September, the company announced it was severing all ties with him in September and would no longer restock his back catalogue and some bookshops have sought to return unsold copies of his work.

Decisions about whether schools or libraries should stock his work is ultimately left up to them.

Asked whether the star's books would be removed from South Gloucestershire Council libraries and schools, a spokesperson said:

"It would be something for the individual schools rather than for us to issue a directive, and our libraries are guided by the LibrariesWest Collection Development Policy."

A spokesperson for Somerset Council said that "Decisions about library stock continue to be made in line with our existing policies and normal library processes."

Councillor Stephen Williams, Chair of the Public Health and Communities Committee at Bristol City Council, said:

"Our approach to library collections has not changed.

We provide a balanced range of stock in line with our Collection Development Policy and have no plans to remove the David Walliams titles currently held in our libraries.

Decisions about books stocked in school libraries are a matter for individual schools."

Gloucestershire County Council are not part of LibrariesWest but say they also have no plans to ban books by Walliams.

"People can decide what they do or don't want to read, and we recognise that everyone will have their own views and make their own choices," said Councillor Paul Hodgkinson, cabinet member responsible for libraries at Gloucestershire County Council.

"Our role as a library service is to provide a wide range of books and give readers the freedom to make those choices for themselves.

"We regularly review and refresh our collections based on what people want to read. Demand for these books has fallen in recent years, so we would expect the number of copies available to reduce naturally over time."

articles.title: Hebbal tunnel alignment threatens 92 tree & 199 bird species, finds rapid environmental impact assessment by Azim Premji University
articles.summary: Rapid EIA by Azim Premji University warns Bengaluru’s Hebbal tunnel alignment may affect 92 tree species and 199 bird species, including vulnerable eagle.
articles.body: Bengaluru: The proposed Hebbal short tunnel alignment passes through an ecologically rich area where 92 tree species and 199 bird species have been recorded, including two bird species of conservation significance, a rapid environmental impact assessment by Azim Premji University researchers has found.Researchers Harini Nagendra, Seema Mundoli, Prachi Gupta and Vivek G surveyed 1,128 trees along the 2.2km alignment for removal or transplantation. The inventory includes 36 trees with girths ranging from 200cm to 800cm, including a banyan with an 800cm girth and a Mysore fig with a 600cm girth.The survey identified 63 Madras thorn trees, 31 jamun and 13 jackfruit trees. Flowering species included 67 Pongamia, 57 gulmohar, 45 yellow copperpods and 30 rain trees. Other species included guava, tamarind, coconut, Singapore cherry and gooseberry. The trees have collectively sequestered an estimated 77 metric tonnes of carbon.Data from eBird and iNaturalist showed 199 bird species recorded in the area over the past decade. They included the greater spotted eagle, classified as vulnerable, and the spot-billed pelican, classified as near threatened on the IUCN Red List. About 50 waterbird species were recorded around Hebbal Lake.The Oct 21 assessment covered 12 stretches. It identified 165 trees marked for removal within Hebbal Lake premises along Ballari Road and another 159 within University of Agricultural Sciences staff quarters.
